title: Wood beats stone in quakes? This 67 m pagoda has stood since 1056 | China Travel Expert
description:
Wood beats stone in an earthquake? This timber pagoda has done exactly that since 1056.

The Yingxian Wooden Pagoda (Sakyamuni Pagoda of Fogong Temple, Shanxi) is 67.31 m of timber built in 1056 — with almost no nails. Four structural tricks keep it standing: interlocking dougong brackets, two rings of columns that form a composite tube, four hidden mezzanine floors braced into stiff rings (5 storeys outside, 9 levels inside), and a frame that sways instead of snapping. The diagrams are drawn by us, step by step — a schematic, not a survey.

🧭 Expert Tip: In recent years only the ground floor has been open to visitors — come for the exterior and the dougong brackets up close, and check access before you travel.

Sources (checked 2026-10-23):
• Built 1056, 67.31 m, 30.27 m base, no iron nails / mortise-and-tenon, ~54 types of dougong, survived many earthquakes and 1920s shelling — China Daily 'Wooden pagoda stands test of time' (2025-07-28): https://regional.chinadaily.com.cn/shanxi/2025-07/28/c_1112835.htm + Guinness World Records 'Largest wooden pagoda'.
• 5 storeys outside / 9 levels inside (五明四暗); hidden floors braced with diagonal struts into rigid rings; dougong joints with gaps buffer and dissipate seismic energy — Tsinghua University (清华新闻): https://www.tsinghua.edu.cn/info/1182/51169.htm
• Composite tube structure (复合筒式结构); bracket-type counts quoted 54–75, hence '50+' on screen — The Paper/CCTV: https://m.thepaper.cn/detail/31652924

Wording guard: 'almost no nails' (sources disagree on 'zero'); '50+ bracket types' (54/59/75 across sources); no earthquake count claimed.
